01.title: Creating My ePortfolio
01.summary: Setting up my ITC-C508 portfolio and writing my initial responses and expectations for the course.
01.skills: This activity helped me organize academic work into a portfolio that readers can navigate easily. I connected my initial understanding of deep learning and NLP to practical examples, including customer churn and conversational systems. I also considered how typography, page structure, and supporting files can make my learning clearer to someone viewing the website for the first time. I also practiced connecting a written explanation to the actual output so the reader can follow what the activity is about.
01.importance: A portfolio gives my activities context instead of leaving them as separate files. It lets me explain what each output shows and why it matters to my development as an IT student. Writing my course expectations also gives me a starting point that I can compare with the projects and skills I develop later in the semester. Keeping these early expectations gives me a way to look back and see which goals the later activities helped me work toward.
01.reflection:
At the start of the course, I wanted to understand how computers learn from data and work with language. Writing my expectations helped me connect these ideas to things like customer service and chatbots. Making the portfolio also help me see why my work needs a clear explanation, not just a file attached.

Another thing I considered is how someone else will view my work. If the activities are difficult to find or the descriptions are unclear, the reader might not understand what the output is showing. This makes the portfolio part of my learning too, because I need to choose the evidence and explain its connection to the course. I want the pages to be simple enough to read while still showing the process behind the activities.

For now, I want to keep my activities organized and explain what I learned from each one. Later on, I hope I can use this portfolio to show how my technical and design skills have improved.

02.skills: I learned how text is broken into tokens, prepared for analysis, and represented in ways a computer can process. The Microsoft Learn activity introduced concepts such as TF-IDF, word embeddings, and entity recognition. Using the language and chat playgrounds helped me distinguish between extracting specific information from a document and generating an answer to a question. The examples helped me see why the same text may need different treatment depending on whether the task is classification, extraction, or generation.
02.importance: NLP is useful in systems that handle customer messages, search documents, or assist people through conversation. The PII extraction exercise also showed how language tools can help identify sensitive information in business documents. As an IT student, understanding these tasks helps me choose an approach that fits a problem instead of treating every language-related feature as the same kind of chatbot. It also reminds me to consider what information a system needs to preserve, especially when handling personal details or words that change the meaning.
02.reflection:
Before this activity, I mostly knew NLP from the apps I use, but I didn't really understand what happens behind them. The playground exercises made it easier to follow because I could see the results myself. One thing I learned is that removing words isn't always helpful, especially when a word like ‘not’ changes the meaning.

The PII extraction exercise was a useful example because it showed a specific task, finding personal information in a document. The chat playground showed a different use of language, where the system generates a response. Comparing them helped me understand that NLP covers several tasks, and the method should depend on what the application needs. I also want to be more careful in checking the output, since a response looking complete doesn't automatically mean every detail is correct.

I still need more practice preparing text and checking what information gets lost. This activity help me understand the basics that I can use when we start making more complicated language applications.

03.skills: I trained a text classifier using labeled examples of customer feedback and tested it with sentences outside the training set. The activity helped me distinguish Positive Praise, Negative Complaint, and Urgent Support. I also practiced checking incorrect predictions, adding more varied examples, and comparing results across testing rounds rather than relying on a single successful prediction. This gave me practice looking at the meaning of a message rather than assuming that one familiar word is enough to decide its category.
03.importance: Automatically organizing feedback can help a business notice complaints and urgent concerns sooner. However, a model needs examples that represent how customers actually communicate, including indirect wording and sarcasm. This activity showed why a classifier should be evaluated on unfamiliar messages before its predictions are used to support customer service decisions. Checking these difficult cases can help prevent urgent messages from being overlooked and makes the evaluation more useful than a test with only straightforward examples.
03.reflection:
I noticed that the model's mistakes were connected to the examples I gave it. Some messages were harder to classify because they used sarcasm or different wording. Adding more examples helped me understand why having enough training data matters. It also showed me that a positive word doesn't always mean the whole message is positive.

What I found useful was checking the sentences the model got wrong instead of only looking at the overall accuracy. Those examples can show whether the problem comes from unclear labels, missing kinds of feedback, or wording that the model hasn't learned well. In another version of the activity, I would keep a separate list of these difficult examples and use new test messages to check whether the changes actually helped. This would make the comparison more useful than testing only familiar sentences.

My next goal is to use more varied test sentences and keep track of the common mistakes. The results gives me a better idea of what I should improve before trusting the model on new messages.

04.skills: I worked with a TensorFlow/Keras pipeline that converts text into numerical sequences, divides data into training and evaluation sets, and trains a neural network. I explored learning rate, hidden-layer size, dropout, batch size, and epochs. Reading loss curves and validation metrics helped me compare configurations and recognize when a model was not generalizing well. The notebook and workbook also helped me connect the settings used in a run with the metrics and charts produced after training.
04.importance: Training accuracy alone does not show whether a model will handle new customer messages correctly. Validation results, F1-scores, and loss curves provide different views of performance. The activity also showed that improving the amount and variety of training data can be more useful than repeatedly changing settings while keeping an inenough dataset. Being able to explain these differences is useful when deciding whether the next step should be better data, another experiment, or a change in the model.
04.reflection:
At first, I thought changing the settings would be enough to improve the model. After comparing the experiments, I understood that the amount and variety of data also makes a big difference. The training log helped me compare the results instead of just remembering which run looked better.

The loss curves also gave me another way to understand the training. A model can keep improving on the training data while the validation result stops improving, so I shouldn't judge a run using one number alone. I need to consider the dataset, the settings, and how the results change together. For another experiment, I would make the comparisons more systematic and clearly separate the effect of changing the data from the effect of changing a hyperparameter.

I want to be more organized when testing, especially in recording what I changed and why. In future projects, I hope I can explain the results better and choose settings based on the evaluation, not just because they seem good.

05.title: Preliminary Long Quiz
05.summary: A checkpoint for reviewing the concepts introduced during the preliminary term.
05.skills: This checkpoint connects to the preliminary term’s topics: NLP concepts, learning from labeled examples, and neural network training. Reviewing these topics means distinguishing what a model learns from data, how text becomes numerical input, and how training settings affect performance. These are the ideas I need to explain clearly alongside the practical activities. I can use the earlier outputs as examples when reviewing the difference between preparing data, training a model, and checking its predictions.
05.importance: A quiz gives me another way to check understanding from following a notebook or completing a guided exercise. It encourages me to organize the concepts and identify which explanations still need work. The value of this checkpoint is in using it to guide further review, rather than treating the activity as an isolated requirement. It also helps me plan my review more clearly by focusing on concepts I cannot yet explain, rather than rereading every topic in the same way.
05.reflection: This quiz is a chance for me to review the NLP and machine learning concepts from Prelims. I want to understand how the ideas connect to our activities, instead of just remembering the definitions. It also help me identify which topics I still need to go back to before moving on to the next lessons.

06.skills: The preliminary examination is a checkpoint for the foundation developed through the term’s NLP and neural network activities. The related skills include interpreting technical concepts, connecting them to examples, and explaining the purpose of stages in a learning pipeline. The uploaded examination photos preserve the assessment record alongside the practical reports and notebooks. Reviewing the assessment together with those outputs can help me connect a definition from class to a concrete step in the work.
06.importance: Keeping the examination in my portfolio helps show that my course work includes both practical outputs and formal assessment. It gives me another point to look back on when reviewing my understanding of the preliminary topics. Together with the activity reports, it can guide which concepts I should revisit before moving into more complex chatbot and retrieval tasks. This record is also useful for looking back at what the course covered before the focus moved toward document-based chatbot systems.
06.reflection: The Prelim exam is a checkpoint for my understanding of the first part of the course. Looking back at our activities helps me connect the concepts to examples, especially in text classification and model training. I still need more practice explaining some ideas clearly, so I want to use the exam and my notes as a guide for what to review.

08.skills: I built a domain-specific RAG chatbot using a curated set of Arcane lore documents. I learned how document preparation, embeddings, vector retrieval, and a language model fit into a single pipeline. I also tested questions outside the knowledge base to examine whether the chatbot could recognize when the supplied information did not support an answer. Following the saved questions and outputs also helped me see where to inspect the system when the final answer does not match the source.
08.importance: A chatbot can produce a fluent response without having enough evidence to support it. Retrieving passages gives the system relevant material, but the answer still needs to be checked against those passages. This is useful for document-based assistants because users need to know whether a response comes from the knowledge base or goes beyond it. A source-based assistant should make it easier to check information, so tracing an answer back to the retrieved material is part of evaluating its usefulness.
08.reflection:
The difficult part for me was understanding how all the parts of the RAG chatbot work together. Following the question from retrieval to the final prompt made the process easier to understand. Testing questions outside the documents also helped me see why a chatbot should know when it doesn't have enough information.

I also realized that a wrong answer can come from different stages. The retriever might miss the relevant information, or the model might receive the right passage but still use it incorrectly. This means I need to inspect the evidence as well as the response before deciding what to change. For another version, I would keep clearer records of the question, retrieved passages, and final answer so I can compare failures and avoid changing settings without knowing the cause.

This activity help me look beyond whether the answer sounds correct. I want to practice checking the retrieved passages first, and later build chatbots that can explain where their answers came from.

09.title: Preliminary ePortfolio Review
09.summary: Organizing the preliminary activities and reflecting on the first part of the course through my earlier portfolio.
09.skills: Organizing the preliminary portfolio involved bringing together NLP exercises, classification work, and neural network experiments. I practiced summarizing what each output demonstrated and connecting the evidence to a reflection. Presenting related activities together also helped show the progression from introductory concepts to training and evaluating a model. I also practiced choosing which details to include so the description explains the output without copying the whole report onto the page.
09.importance: A portfolio should help a reader understand the work without needing to reconstruct the semester from file names. Clear descriptions and reflections make the evidence easier to interpret. Reviewing the preliminary activities also creates a reference point for the midterm tasks, where the focus moves toward retrieval, chatbot behavior, and a group project proposal. It gives me a record of the concepts I understood at that point and the skills I wanted to develop in the next part of the course.
09.reflection:
Putting my Prelim activities together helped me see how the topics were connected. The NLP exercises introduced the basics, then the classification and training activities showed how data affects the results. The activities was easier to explain when I looked at them as part of the same learning process.

The portfolio review also made me think about how much explanation an artifact needs. A notebook or screenshot can show that an activity was done, but the reflection should explain what I understood from it and what still needs improvement. I want to avoid repeating the same general lesson for every output. Giving each activity a specific example would make the portfolio more useful when I look back at how my understanding developed during the semester.

For now, I want to improve the descriptions and make each output easier to find. Later, I want my portfolio to show my progress and the things I still need to work on, not just the finished requirements.

10.skills: The initial DecisionThree proposal focused on a RAG chatbot for comparing JRU undergraduate curricula. It helped me connect a target user, a document-based problem, and a possible technical approach. The proposal also introduced the need to define research questions, identify trustworthy source documents, and plan how correctness, how well an answer is supported, and completeness would be evaluated. The report and presentation also showed how the same project needs a detailed written explanation and a shorter version that communicates its main direction.
10.importance: A project proposal needs more than an interesting application idea. It should explain what problem is being investigated, what evidence the system can use, and how its performance will be checked. Establishing these limits helps a group make practical implementation choices and avoid promising outcomes that the available documents or evaluation cannot demonstrate. This makes the proposal a reference for later decisions, especially when the group needs to choose which features are necessary and which are outside the study.
10.reflection:
Our first proposal was the starting idea for DecisionThree, so it was still a plan rather than a finished system. It helped me understand that having a chatbot idea isn't enough. We also need a clear problem, reliable documents, and a way to check the answers.

Another lesson from the proposal is that we should separate what we hope the system can do from what our study can actually demonstrate. A chatbot might be intended to help students find information, but that doesn't automatically prove that it improves their decisions. We need questions and evaluation criteria that match the claims we make. Keeping this distinction clear would help us write a more realistic report and avoid presenting a planned benefit as an already tested result.

The proposal also help me see why the features should match what we can actually test. My next goal is to keep the project realistic. In future projects, I want to get better at explaining why we chose a solution and how we will know if it works.

11.skills: The updated proposal refined DecisionThree into a program and curriculum inquiry chatbot for graduating Grade 12 students considering JRU CSE. I learned to distinguish included information from excluded topics, such as live schedules or personalized program recommendations. The revised document also made source checking, question design, and the meaning of correctness and how well an answer is supported more explicit. Comparing the versions helped me identify which assumptions were being narrowed and how the revised questions better matched the intended inquiry task.
11.importance: A narrower scope makes it easier to decide whether a chatbot’s answer is relevant and supported. It also helps manage expectations when documents do not contain the requested information. Revising the proposal showed how clear boundaries can guide the interface, knowledge base, and evaluation instead of leaving each part of the project to develop independently. These limits also make it easier to explain why a question needs clarification or why the system should acknowledge that the answer is unavailable.
11.reflection:
Comparing the first and updated proposals helped me understand why narrowing the scope matters. Our focus became more specific, from curriculum comparisons to questions supported by the JRU documents. The changes makes it clearer what the chatbot should answer and what it should leave out.

The updated scope also helped explain why some questions should be left unanswered. If tuition, live schedules, or personal recommendations are outside the approved documents, the chatbot shouldn't make an answer just to be helpful. This affects both the prompt and the interface, because users need to understand those limits. For me, a practical improvement is to keep the same scope consistent across the proposal, the source files, the test questions, and the information shown to the user.

I want to keep these limits clear when preparing the sources and designing the interface. In the long term, I hope I can use feedback better and turn a broad idea into a project that is easier to build and evaluate.

12.skills: The midterm examination provides an assessment record for the stage when the course moved into RAG and project planning. The related skills include explaining retrieval and generation as separate stages, understanding the role of document evidence, and connecting a proposed solution to its evaluation. These ideas also connect to the chatbot notebook and proposal outputs. Reviewing these ideas means being able to explain how a failure in one stage can affect the response produced by the whole pipeline.
12.importance: The exam adds to the practical group and individual activities by creating another checkpoint for reviewing understanding. Keeping the exam evidence with the midterm outputs helps show the different kinds of work completed during the term. It also gives me a reference for identifying concepts to revisit before the more detailed retrieval and optimization experiments in Finals. The assessment and practical work can be used together when deciding which parts of retrieval and evaluation need more review before the final project.
12.reflection: The Midterm exam helped me look back at the lessons about RAG and chatbot development. One idea I want to remember is that an answer sounding correct doesn't mean it has enough support from the documents. Reviewing these topics also help me prepare for the final activities, where we need to test and explain the system's results more carefully.

14.skills: I reviewed and explained the vector indexing notebook, prepared the IT and Business Analytics source, and examined how text becomes searchable chunks. The activity introduced controlled chunk-size and overlap comparisons using FAISS. It also required source-backed questions and prompt boundaries so that the chatbot would distinguish BSIT from BSIT-BA and acknowledge information missing from the document. I also practiced keeping the question, expected answer, and source location connected so the later results could be checked against the same information.
14.importance: A retrieval system depends on how well the source text survives extraction and splitting. Curriculum information can lose meaning when a course code, program label, or related requirement is separated from its context. This activity showed why checking extracted chunks and preparing verified questions are necessary before judging whether the generated answer is useful. If these checks are skipped, a low score may come from a damaged source representation rather than the retrieval setting being tested.
14.reflection:
This activity helped me connect the notebook code to the actual information someone might ask about. I realized that the source document needs attention too, because the chatbot depends on what gets extracted and retrieved. The explanations and page references makes the process easier to follow.

The source preparation also showed why similar program names and repeated course information need careful handling. A passage can contain a matching keyword but still refer to the wrong program or requirement. Before depending on a retrieval result, I need to check the program label, the page reference, and whether the related details remain together. For future work, I would spend more time inspecting the extracted tables and sample chunks before running a larger comparison.

For the next step, I want to check whether the chunks still contain the details needed for each question. I also want more practice preparing documents with tables and similar program names, since those details can affect the answer.

15.skills: I compared twelve chunk-size and overlap configurations using the same nine questions and the same embedding model. I practiced interpreting Precision@3, Recall@3, and MRR@3, checking retrieved evidence, and recording results in a workbook. The experiment also helped me distinguish retrieval evaluation from answer generation: the scores measured which evidence was found, not the quality of a generated response. Keeping the questions and embeddings fixed helped me understand why a controlled comparison is needed when studying the effect of chunking choices.
15.importance: Choosing a retrieval setting should be based on more than the highest score in a small test. The report found that C10 and C12 tied on the main metrics, while C10 used fewer chunks. However, complete evidence was retrieved for only one of nine questions under either configuration. That limitation matters when deciding whether a setting is ready to support a real inquiry system. The experiment therefore gives a starting point for improvement, rather than proof that a single chunk setting will work well for every document or question.
15.reflection:
What stood out to me was that the best configuration in our test still had weak results overall. Tuning the chunk size didn't solve all the problems with extracting curriculum tables and keeping related facts together. The results also shows why I should check the failed questions, not just the highest score.

The tie between C10 and C12 was another useful part of the analysis. Since the main scores were the same, the number of chunks helped explain why C10 was the more efficient option within that comparison. However, that recommendation still needed to include the low overall retrieval coverage. I learned that reporting a winner without explaining the failed questions can make the result sound better than it is. A better next experiment should address those failures, especially the questions needing facts from curriculum tables.

My next goal is to improve the source structure and look at the errors one by one. In the long term, I want to use more questions and better document preparation before calling a retrieval setting reliable.

16.skills: The group experiment compared chunking and retrieval settings and measured matched CPU and GPU workloads. I developed my understanding of response timing, repeated trials, warm-up exclusions, and the difference between retrieval quality and generation quality. Working with the results also required keeping the revised-prompt and prepared-source follow-ups separate from the original comparisons so their effects were not confused. The records helped connect summary tables to the actual trial settings and distinguish repeated measurements from additional independent test questions.
16.importance: A faster chatbot is useful only if its answers remain accurate and supported. The report showed a substantial GPU speed improvement, while the selected revised-prompt configuration still had answer and retrieval errors. Reporting both findings helps explain the tradeoff honestly and prevents a good timing result from being mistaken for proof that the system is reliable. This is especially important when explaining whether an observed improvement applies only to the tested setup or might need more evidence before a wider claim is made.
16.reflection:
This activity showed me why experiment records need to be clear. Changing the hardware, prompt, source, or retrieval settings can affect the results, so it's important to know what was changed in each test. The saved measurements helps explain which improvements we actually observed.

I also learned to look at what a timing measurement includes. Setup, model loading, indexing, and the response itself are different parts of using a system, so the report should be clear about which part was measured. The prompt and source follow-ups also need to stay separate from the matched hardware comparisons. This helped me understand that a fair explanation of performance depends on the experiment design and records, not just a fast number in the results table.

For now, I want to keep every summary connected to its original data and settings. Later, I want to improve how I explain the balance between speed and answer quality, especially when a faster response can still contain mistakes.

17.title: Final Quiz and Examination
17.summary: A final assessment checkpoint for reviewing the semester’s machine learning, retrieval, and evaluation concepts.
17.skills: This checkpoint connects the semester’s progression from text processing and classification to document retrieval and chatbot evaluation. The skills to review include explaining pipeline stages, interpreting experiment settings, and distinguishing a supported answer from a fluent but incorrect one. It also connects the technical terms used in class to the practical notebooks and reports in this portfolio. Reviewing these connections also means knowing which evidence to inspect when a result is unclear, instead of immediately changing the model or its settings.
17.importance: Reviewing the whole semester helps connect topics that were introduced in separate activities. Data preparation affects training, source preparation affects retrieval, and evaluation determines what can be claimed about a result. Treating the final assessment as a checkpoint across these connections can guide further learning beyond the completion of the course requirements. It helps me organize what I should keep practicing after the course, particularly the parts where completing a workflow is easier than explaining its behavior.
17.reflection: This final checkpoint brings together the topics from the whole semester. Looking back at the activities, I can connect the early lessons on data and model training to our later work on retrieval and chatbot evaluation. There are still parts I need to practice, but the portfolio gives me examples to review and build on in my next projects.

18.skills: The final DecisionThree project brought together source preparation, retrieval, answer generation, interface design, and evaluation. My responsibilities focused on preparing source material, the JRU interface, and the results workbook. These areas connected document checking and page mapping with readable source panels and the clear presentation of measured results. The project also strengthened my understanding of how to distinguish speed, answer correctness, and support from the documents. My assigned areas also required keeping the source references, interface information, and result summaries consistent with the evidence described in the final report.
18.importance: A university inquiry assistant needs more than a usable interface and quick responses. The final report recorded success on 7 of 16 questions under the evaluation criteria, including difficulty handling information absent from the source. Presenting those limits matters because readers should verify requirements in the handbook rather than assume that every chatbot answer is trustworthy. The project shows why an interface should help users inspect the evidence and understand the source limits, especially when the information could influence their questions about a program.
18.reflection:
My responsibilities connected source preparation, the JRU interface, and the results workbook. The source work needed attention to scope and page references. The interface side also connected to my interest in UI/UX, while the workbook showed me why the summaries need to match the saved results. These parts was connected even though they involved different tasks.

Even though each of us had a specific responsibility, we didn't just focus on our own task and leave the rest to the others. We helped each other in every part of the project, shared ideas, and checked the work together. This also help me understand how my part connects to the other parts of the system. For me, the assigned tasks gave us a clear starting point, but working together was still important in bringing the whole project together.

The final evaluation made this lesson more concrete. Our report recorded success on 7 out of 16 questions under the project criteria, so it would be wrong to describe the chatbot as dependable just because the interface works and the response time is faster. The questions with missing information were especially important because the system still needed to avoid making unsupported answers. From my side, clear source panels, organized results, and visible limitations can help people inspect the output, while further work is still needed on the source handling and answer behavior.

My biggest takeaway is that a clear design can help people inspect an answer, but it can't make an unsupported answer correct. For now, I want to improve the source structure and explain the limitations more clearly. In the long term, I want to design interfaces that help people understand and check the information they receive.
